newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB expected to stress Swiss growth on Friday.
newsitem.headline: SNB expected to stress Swiss growth on Friday.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) will keep the focus on stagnant economic growth and make clear at its annual news conference on Friday that it will extend its generous monetary policy into next year, analysts said.
It may may well avoid fixing a precise projection for 1997 money supply growth to give itself more leeway to act in a difficult environment, they said.

Hans Scherer, currency analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland, ruled out any move to clamp down on growth in benchmark seasonally adjusted central bank money supply M0, which includes banknotes in circulation and sight deposits at the SNB.

"You have to remember, even though it (M0) is overshooting now, over the last five years it has undershot. There is a situation of economic gloom in Switzerland. It is right that the SNB plumps up the (M0)," Scherer said.
"If they were to indicate that they would tighten, it would be inopportune right now. The economy is still in the doldrums," he added.

"I think what they (the SNB) will stress is that there are times in conducting monetary policy where you need to be more flexible. You need to pay some attention to the real economy and to the exchange rate as well," said Swiss Bank Corp's Jan Acket.
He said he would be surprised if SNB Chairman Hans Meyer announced a specific projection for M0.

"The markets are very much focused on what the SNB currently does. Giving any figure would centre the expectation on a particular growth rate in M0. I don't think they want to do that currently," Acket said.
"They (the SNB) need the leeway to achieve their goal to appear to be still expansionist," he said.
The SNB stopped fixing a formal annual money supply target in 1990 but continues to aim at a money supply growth path that will guarantee a stable price level.
Since 1990, the SNB has followed a policy of setting a medium-term growth path for M0. The current period runs from January 1995 to the end of 1999.
Growth in the base has been set at roughly one percent per year over the period, a rate seen adequate to keep the economy growing without inflation.
M0 growth has been above that level this year. The SNB has said it expects it to be between 4.0 and 4.5 percent at the end of the fourth quarter compared with the year-earlier quarter.

Meyer faces the difficult task of satisfying politicians, trade unions, exporters and investors worried about weak domestic growth. He also has to convince financial markets that the SNB has not lost its grip on inflation.
He will also have to take care not to upset the delicate balance in currency markets, where the Swiss franc has fallen to nearly two-year lows gainst the dollar and mark.
Its decline from inflated levels in the mid-1990s partly reflect the SNB's more expansive policy, which it launched in mid-1995 and stepped up in August.
Meyer took over this year from Markus Lusser, who said last December the central bank would aim again for seasonally adjusted M0 to grow in 1996 at a rate from one to two percent.
Meyer must also beware of destabilising the balance which the SNB has struck between an expansionary policy and a long-term commitment to price stability.
The SNB expects domestic inflation of about one to 1.5 percent in 1996. The economy, which has basically stagnated since 1990, is expected to shrink this year.

Some SNB officials say Swiss real gross domestic product (GDP) growth may be weaker than 1.0 percent next year, a level which analysts say is too low to stimulate jobs growth at a time unemployment is nearing post-war highs near five percent.

GDP fell an annualised 0.7 percent in the third quarter on both a quarterly and year-on-year basis. The government's official advisory panel has forecast 0.5 percent real growth in 1997 after a 1996 decline of 0.75 percent.
